title: This Singing Lemur Uses the Same Trick as Opera Stars
summary:
Have you ever heard an opera singer hit a really high note? They open their mouths wide to make the sound carry. Now scientists have found a lemur that does the exact same thing.

The indri is the world's only known singing lemur. It lives in Madagascar's rainforest and makes piercing, siren-like calls that travel long distances. These songs help keep its family group together and warn other lemurs to stay away.

Researchers studied 83 video recordings of 19 wild indris. They tracked the lemurs' lips frame by frame. What did they find? Every time the pitch went up, the lemur opened its mouth wider. That's the same technique opera singers use — it's called "formant tuning."

"It's the kind of fine-tuned coordination between voice and body that we usually associate with trained human singers, not with a lemur singing from the forest canopy," said Chiara De Gregorio, a study co-author.

Here's the wild part: humans and indris last shared a common ancestor about 74 million years ago. That's before dinosaurs went extinct! So the two species didn't copy each other — they each came up with the same solution on their own. Scientists call that "convergent evolution." Nature is full of surprises!
why_it_matters: It reminds us that humans aren't the only ones who can do clever things with sound — and that animals solving problems in the same way we do is a clue to how hard problems get solved again and again in nature.

background_read: Madagascar (a large island country off the east coast of Africa) is home to animals found nowhere else on Earth, such as lemurs.
Opera singers train for years to open their mouths wide on high notes so their voice can reach the back of a huge hall.
The indri is the biggest living lemur, and its siren-like song carries far through the rainforest — which is why scientists could record and study it.
Article_Structure: WHO: Researchers who filmed indris in the wild, including study co-author Chiara De Gregorio
WHAT: They watched 83 videos of 19 wild indris and found that the lemurs open their mouths wider as their pitch rises — the same 'formant tuning' trick opera singers use
WHERE: The rainforest of Madagascar, where the indri sings from the forest canopy
WHY: It shows convergent evolution — humans and indris each invented the same singing technique on their own after their last common ancestor about 74 million years ago

perspectives.description: They think it is exciting that a wild animal uses the same singing technique as trained human opera stars.
Voice teachers can point out that the 'formant tuning' trick they teach has been used by lemurs for millions of years.
They warn that the indris were only filmed, not tested in a lab, so scientists still need more proof about how the lemurs control their voices.
